quarterly_data.signal: Memory: demand improved sequentially for DRAM and HBM applications in Q4, and management expects the momentum to extend into 2026 as customers expand capacity for AI-related demand. Axcelis secured an order for a high current system from a leading North American memory manufacturer (not named), which broadens its presence beyond its strong position in Korea; the order arrived before an existing system evaluation was complete, which management views as an endorsement of the technology. Q4 bookings were led by power, general mature and memory (specifically DRAM), and the 2026 memory business, led by DRAM, is expected to grow and offset lower power and general mature revenue.

CEO: DRAM demand keeps rising, driven by AI, but capacity is limited by cleanroom space. Many customers are squeezing in an extra couple of tools, and large tool volumes will come only when the new fabs open. DRAM is expected to be significantly up in 2026 over a lower 2025 base, with momentum into 2027 across all DRAM manufacturers as the cleanroom bottleneck eases. As an example he cited SK hynix's Yongin cluster, '4 mega fabs of 200,000 wafer starts a week', where he expects SK hynix to start taking systems around early 2027 to ramp the fabs. DRAM prices are spiking because supply is very constrained.
quarterly_data.figure: SK hynix Yongin cluster (cited as an example): '4 mega fabs of 200,000 wafer starts a week' (as spoken); taking systems early 2027

quarterly_data.signal: Implant capital intensity: for DRAM, customers typically spend about $150 million to $200 million on implant equipment for every 100,000 wafer starts brought online. Most of that is high current, with a little high energy. NAND and DRAM requirements are mostly similar, but the split between high energy, high current and medium current varies. Axcelis already has a very good position in high energy and is building on its high current position, which is why management is positive on high current.
quarterly_data.figure: $150 million to $200 million of implant capital per 100,000 wafer starts (DRAM)

quarterly_data.signal: Memory ordering and sizing: memory usually books and ships in the same quarter, so little memory sits in backlog. Customers give multi-quarter long-range forecasts that have historically been sound (sometimes exceeded) and are currently quite positive, with purchase orders placed a week to a quarter ahead. Management gave no 2026 memory revenue figure but called 2026 growth a healthy number off a fairly low 2025 base, with acceleration into 2027 depending on wafer starts and fab expansions. Prior peaks: the CEO recalled the last highest memory year as about $120 million (NAND and DRAM combined), and the CFO said the last DRAM high was $90 million, set before the North American memory manufacturer win. Memory systems carry lower gross margins than the rest of the mix.
quarterly_data.figure: last DRAM high $90 million; last highest memory year about $120 million (NAND and DRAM)

quarterly_data.signal: NAND: customers remain focused on higher layer counts, which do not add ion implant demand, so NAND demand is expected to stay muted in the near term and through 2026. It could free up in 2027, depending on what capacity NAND producers need. Recent improvements in NAND bit demand and pricing are encouraging, and management says customers resuming wafer capacity additions is a matter of when, not if.

Q4 2025 revenue was $238 million: systems $156 million and CS&I a quarterly record $82 million, both above outlook. The beat came from stronger CS&I aftermarket revenue (upgrade demand plus some pull-in from Q1 as utilization improved). Non-GAAP gross margin was 47.3% against a 43% outlook, on a higher CS&I and upgrade mix. Non-GAAP operating margin was 21.1%, adjusted EBITDA $55 million and non-GAAP EPS $1.49 against a $1.12 outlook. China fell to 32% of revenue from 46% in the prior quarter as customers digest mature-node capacity; Europe was 15%, the U.S. 14%, Korea 13%, Japan 9% and Taiwan 3%. Bookings rose significantly quarter over quarter to $128 million, led by power, general mature and memory (specifically DRAM); general mature and power remain the main parts of bookings.
quarterly_data.figure: revenue $238 million; systems $156 million; CS&I $82 million; non-GAAP gross margin 47.3%; non-GAAP EPS $1.49; China 32%; bookings $128 million

quarterly_data.signal: Full year 2025: non-GAAP gross margin was 45.2%, up 30 basis points despite lower revenue, on favorable mix and cost control. Adjusted EBITDA was $177 million, non-GAAP EPS $4.88 and free cash flow $107 million. Q4 free cash flow was negative $9 million because sales were weighted to December and about $5 million went to Veeco transaction expenses. Upgrades and services both reached record levels in 2025 on a growing installed base. By region, China was 42% of 2025 revenue, the U.S. 16%, Korea 13% and Europe 11%. The company repurchased approximately $121 million of shares in 2025, with $110 million of authorization remaining, and ended Q4 with $557 million of cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities. Veeco merger: shareholders of both companies approved it at special meetings on February 6 and clearance has come in several jurisdictions. China is the final approval needed, and closing is still expected in the second half of 2026.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2025 non-GAAP gross margin 45.2%; adjusted EBITDA $177 million; non-GAAP EPS $4.88; free cash flow $107 million; cash and securities $557 million

quarterly_data.signal: Q1 2026 outlook: revenue approximately $195 million, down quarter over quarter. Systems are lower because a few shipments were pushed out by the timing of customers' available cleanroom space (fab readiness), and CS&I is lower on Q4 seasonality, a large Q4 customer upgrade that will not recur and some CS&I pulled forward into Q4. Non-GAAP gross margin approximately 41%, on a higher mix of lower-margin memory systems, a lower CS&I and upgrade mix and a modest tariff impact. Non-GAAP opex approximately $59 million, adjusted EBITDA approximately $26 million, non-GAAP EPS approximately $0.71. Full year 2026: revenue approximately flat versus 2025 and weighted to the second half, as memory growth offsets slightly lower power and general mature revenue; non-GAAP gross margin low to mid-40% on a stronger memory mix, with a tariff impact under 100 basis points; quarterly opex similar to Q1; tax rate approximately 15%.
quarterly_data.figure: Q1 revenue approximately $195 million; non-GAAP gross margin approximately 41%; non-GAAP EPS approximately $0.71; FY2026 revenue approximately flat; FY2026 gross margin low to mid-40%

quarterly_data.signal: Power: silicon carbide shipments eased slightly quarter over quarter as customers stay disciplined on capacity after the earlier build-out and put technology transitions first. A key Q4 CS&I driver was a large customer converting its silicon carbide tools from 150 millimeter to 200 millimeter and, in the same footprint, upgrading them to the recently introduced Purion Power Series+ platform. Only a very small part of the installed base has moved to 200-millimeter, with leaders outside China going first, which leaves ample upgrade opportunity. Select China customers are expanding SiC device capacity, while customers in other regions invest in trench and superjunction, which is driving growing interest in the company's newly developed high-energy channeling capability (essential for superjunction). Near-term SiC implant demand should stay muted while customers absorb capacity. Other power (silicon IGBTs) also eased, and power overall is expected slightly lower in 2026. Longer term, management expects power semiconductors (silicon, silicon carbide and gallium nitride) to benefit from the growing power needs of AI, from wider adoption of 800-volt EVs and from physical AI.
quarterly_data.figure: 150 millimeter to 200 millimeter tool conversion; only a very small part of the installed base at 200-millimeter

quarterly_data.signal: General mature: revenue rose quarter over quarter on select investments, mainly in high current tools. Implant tool utilization improved across multiple customers in Q4, but there is no sign yet of a recovery in capex for mature process technologies: customers must fill their existing tools first, and Axcelis sits further down the supply chain. General mature is expected slightly down in 2026, with 2027 seen as the opportunity. In China, utilization is still high and customers want more capacity to reach self-sufficiency goals they remain far from; the CFO sees China revenue relatively flat to down slightly in 2026 and a durable part of the business. Management also expects physical AI (robotics, autonomous vehicles, edge devices) to lift general mature demand for MCUs, image sensors and analog.
quarterly_data.figure: China 42% of 2025 revenue; China 2026 relatively flat to down slightly

quarterly_data.signal: Advanced logic: Axcelis generated revenue on a follow-on order from an existing customer and is working with customers on next-generation needs, including implant for backside power contacts and other material modification applications. Advanced logic revenue in 2026 is expected to be similar to 2025, because evaluations on next-generation logic architectures will take time to turn into meaningful volume.

Early in the month of the call, the company introduced the Purion H6, its next-generation high current ion implanter. It brings advances across the beam line, source, particle control and dosimetry subsystems, offers industry-leading dose repeatability, and targets high current applications in advanced logic, memory and mature nodes. Q4 was the strongest quarter of high current shipments in 2 years (the CFO clarified it was the high for that 2-year period, not an all-time record), reflecting memory turning on plus a broader base in general mature and power; management sees high current market share rising.
quarterly_data.figure: strongest quarter of high current shipments in 2 years
